clinicalPearls: Acquired haemophilia A is caused by spontaneous autoantibodies, usually IgG, directed against coagulation factor VIII, arising in people with no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder.
Presentation is typically with sudden extensive bruising and soft-tissue, muscle, mucosal or retroperitoneal bleeding; haemarthrosis, so characteristic of congenital haemophilia, is uncommon.

The screening abnormality is an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time, which does not correct on a mixing study, particularly after incubation at body temperature.
Confirmation requires a reduced factor VIII level together with a demonstrable inhibitor quantified by the Bethesda assay.
Recognised associations include advanced age, the postpartum period, autoimmune disease, malignancy and certain drugs, although a large proportion of cases remain idiopathic.

Factor VIII autoantibodies typically show complex (type II) kinetics, so a measurable residual factor VIII level can coexist with severe bleeding and the inhibitor titre does not reliably predict bleeding severity.

Acute bleeding is controlled with bypassing agents such as activated prothrombin complex concentrate or recombinant activated factor VII, or with recombinant porcine factor VIII, rather than with standard human factor VIII.
Definitive treatment requires eradication of the inhibitor with immunosuppression, and care should be shared with a specialist haemophilia centre.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder results from a breakdown of self-tolerance leading to polyclonal IgG autoantibodies against factor VIII, most often targeting the A2 or C2 domains that mediate binding to von Willebrand factor, phospholipid and factor IXa. Neutralisation of factor VIII procoagulant activity impairs the intrinsic tenase complex and thus thrombin generation, producing a bleeding tendency. Unlike the alloantibodies seen in congenital haemophilia, these autoantibodies commonly display second-order (type II) kinetics that do not completely inactivate factor VIII, which explains why residual factor activity may be detectable despite clinically significant haemorrhage. The autoimmune process may be triggered by pregnancy, malignancy, drugs or another autoimmune condition, or may be idiopathic.
additionalDifferentials: congenital haemophilia A with an alloantibody inhibitor
lupus anticoagulant (prolongs the APTT but predisposes to thrombosis, not bleeding)
other acquired specific clotting factor inhibitors
liver disease with impaired synthesis of clotting factors
additionalInvestigations: activated partial thromboplastin time with immediate and incubated mixing studies
Bethesda assay to quantify inhibitor titre
von Willebrand factor antigen and activity
screening for underlying malignancy and autoimmune disease
redFlags: a large or expanding haematoma, particularly retroperitoneal
limb swelling with pain suggesting compartment syndrome or nerve compression
airway or neck swelling threatening the airway
reference.prognosis: Bleeding-related and treatment-related morbidity and mortality are considerable, especially in the elderly and those with comorbidity, but complete remission of the inhibitor is achieved in the majority with immunosuppression; relapse can occur and warrants ongoing follow-up.
pitfalls: misinterpreting the prolonged APTT as a lupus anticoagulant and failing to test for a factor VIII inhibitor
administering standard human factor VIII concentrate and expecting a normal haemostatic response
underestimating bleeding risk from the inhibitor titre or from a measurable residual factor VIII level
delaying immunosuppression, which prolongs the period of bleeding risk
performing intramuscular injections, arterial punctures or invasive procedures without haematological cover
